What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
## Definition

A **nonsquare pixel** is a pixel whose width is not the same size as its height, giving it a rectangular rather than square shape [S3]. The width-to-height relationship of that individual pixel is its **pixel aspect ratio** — the pixel's width divided by its height — which is independent of the overall image's aspect ratio [S10][S1]. Properly adjusted computer monitors have square pixels with a pixel aspect ratio of 1:1 [S1].

## Where it shows up in cinema and video

Nonsquare pixels appear whenever the aspect ratio of the displayed image differs from that of the original digital image [S2]. Standard-definition video is the classic case: NTSC-DV runs 720×480 and PAL-DV 720×576, both with rectangular pixels, while HD, graphics-editing software, and computer monitors all use square pixels [S8]. The book also covers film formats that optically distort the frame, which it calls **squeezed** or **anamorphic** formats, using Cinemascope's dramatic 2:1 squeeze as its main example [S7][S5].

## Technical implications

The practical danger is unaccounted-for stretching. In US NTSC analog video, for instance, the pixel aspect ratio is 10:11 — pixels are slightly taller than they are wide — so a perfectly round digital circle displays as an ellipse stretched vertically by 11/10ths unless the image is scaled to compensate [S13]. Rotation is another trap: rotating an element while it is still squeezed produces wrong results; the correct procedure is to **unsqueeze → rotate → resqueeze** along the x-axis [S9].

## Author's stance and advice

The book is careful to say that "displaying nonsquare pixels" does not mean the physical pixels on your monitor become stretched — the display system merely applies a temporary geometric transformation, leaving the underlying image data untouched [S4]. The author's repeated warnings are to **not confuse pixel aspect ratio with image aspect ratio** [S13], to know whether your software compensates automatically or needs manual scaling [S13], and to "double-check everything" when working with nonsquare pixels so subtle distortions don't slip into the final result [S9].

What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The drawing books in the corpus are full of practical "field notes" for animators and storyboard artists — bold lines, clear silhouettes, one idea per sketch, and a strong emphasis on feeling the pose. Grouped by theme, the tips are:

## Line quality and tools
- Draw **BOLD** with a grease pencil, marker, or 2B pencil — never a hard pencil — and **number your drawings** so they read from across the room [S2].
- You should be able to **blacken in a drawing and still read what is happening**; keep decoration inside the main outline, and make the outlines themselves interesting [S1][S22].
- Play **straight lines against curves** for visual interest [S3]. Use straight-line symbols for stretches and bent lines for squashes [S6].
- Use drybrush (speed lines) **very sparingly** — only when drawings are spaced so widely the eye struggles to connect them; good spacing and anticipated action let the eye bridge wide gaps on its own [S4][S21].

## Clarity and composition
- **One idea per sketch** — "draw attention to one idea at a time, just like when speaking" [S3][S7]. Highlight the important idea and subordinate everything else to it [S6].
- Draw borders so you're forced to compose within them [S6]. Avoid symmetry ("it is boring… makes drawings look cut out") and use angles instead [S6].
- **Don't get too clever** — tricky camera angles often just make the drawing ambiguous [S6]. Camera framing and transitions matter for storytelling: the same elements can deliver very different messages depending on shot composition [S30].

## Expression and observation
- Show **how the character feels**: feel the pose, the emotion, kinetically in your own body — a person is always "doing" something, so express the purpose [S6].
- Watch the body's **landmarks where bones reach the surface**, like hipbones and ribs [S6]; darken pupils when drawing eyes [S3].
- Learning to draw has two halves: **technique** (perspective, anatomy, force, shape) and **honest observation** — combine them, and diagnose your own work: generic? look more. Flat and dead? use technique [S5][S19].
- Drawing **multiple moments** of the same subject tells more about personality than a single drawing [S10][S25]. Chiaroscuro reminds you the outline "never existed" anyway — you're describing light and form [S13][S23].
- For faces, even subtle muscular differences matter — e.g., in the Facial Action Coding System, AU 18 (lip pucker) vs. AU 35 (cheek suck-in) differ by whether the cheeks are actually pulled inward [S11][S14].

## Process habits
- **Always rough-sketch first** — the sketch clarifies the image and the "appearance/state" of what you'll draw [S9].
- Don't be afraid to **redraw and rework**: if part of a drawing doesn't work, cut it out and try again [S3].
- Draw many sections, and build toward storyboard pitching once the boards are complete [S12][S17].

## Context for cinema
The tips are aimed squarely at animation and storyboard work, where drawings must survive projection: bold lines and readable silhouettes ensure a board "reads" at a distance, one-idea-per-sketch keeps shots unambiguous, and avoiding tricky camera angles keeps the action legible on screen [S1][S2][S6]. Timing guidance from the animation side — anticipation on drawings 1–5, overshoot on 6–9, settling on 10–12 — speaks to how storyboards communicate motion before any frames are shot [S27].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
**The book's answer: transcoding works when the two displays are nearly identical except for their primary colors; color rerendering is needed when viewing conditions or contrast/white levels are grossly dissimilar.** The deciding factor throughout is simply the degree of difference between source and target display [S1][S2].

| | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **When it applies** | Black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma are identical; only the primaries differ [S2] | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar between displays [S1] |
| **What it does** | Recodes the image from one display's color encoding to another's | Undoes whatever color rendering was done for the first display, then color renders the CIE XYZ values for the second [S1] |
| **Nature of the operation** | Purely mathematical respace | An appearance adjustment for a changed viewing environment [S4] |

Transcoding is the simpler case. Because the displays agree on everything except primaries, the book says you need only linearize the first display's encoded RGB, convert those values to CIE XYZ, convert them to the second display's RGB, and reimpose that display's encoding nonlinearity [S2]:

```text
encoded RGB (display 1) → linearize → CIE XYZ → RGB (display 2) → re-apply nonlinearity
```

Color rerendering (also called "color rendering" in color-management terms) means transforming an image to account for differences in viewing environment — for example, a still camera rendering a scene shot in bright desert sunlight for an office monitor whose peak white is hundreds of times weaker [S4]. When the change in viewing environment is severe, a straight numeric transcode isn't enough; the appearance intent itself must be recalculated [S1].

The book touches on the same idea in ACES: the RRT supplies the appearance rendering (S-curve tone compression, saturation control) for the standard theatrical viewing environment, and the ODT then adapts the rendered data to each display device — effectively institutionalizing "rerendering" per display [S3][S5][S9]. Worth noting that "rendering" also appears in a totally different sense elsewhere in the book — creating merged playback media from timeline effects [S11] — but that's unrelated to this display-to-display question.

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
**The book's core claim: affect, fatigue, and injury are not adjectives you append after choreography is chosen — they are control states that must change later action selection and execution [S24].** They sit below narrative intent (which guides the selection and timing of lower-level controls but cannot be compressed into one fixed pose) and above the raw motion layer [S1]. The book then specifies each state's internal structure, how it updates, and how you verify it was actually respected downstream.

## Affect: dimensional, appraisal-driven, and underdetermined

Affect is modeled as a continuous trajectory on **valence, arousal, and dominance** — answering whether the experience turns more positive or negative, activated or calm, empowered or overwhelmed. It is useful for interpolation and temporal arcs, but it stays underdetermined: the same high-arousal negative state can surface as fear, anger, pain, or disgust depending on appraisal, context, and action tendencies [S1].

The book's worked example is an appraisal update: when an expected interception fails and the north lane opens, goal congruence drops to −0.72, controllability rises to 0.34, certainty to 0.61, and the posterior shifts from {valence −0.20, arousal 0.58, dominance 0.56} to {valence −0.48, arousal 0.76, dominance 0.38}. The declared **behavioral effects** are what make it a control state: attention narrows toward the exit lane, recovery becomes urgent but mechanically less clean, and risk tolerance rises for one recovery attempt [S3]. A companion warning says not to compile "anger = always faster" or "fear = always retreat": kinematic cues to emotion exist at population level, not as a deterministic universal mapping, with character, culture, task, injury, and tactical intent as moderators [S13].

## Fatigue: a compiler state with a recurrence

Fatigue is proposed as a state variable, not remaining capacity, updated by

```
f(r,t+Δ) = clamp(f(r,t) + work(r,t) + impact(r,t) − recovery(r,t), 0, 1)
```

with the caveat that the work, impact, and recovery terms must be calibrated — they are not reliably inferred from prose alone [S4]. The book splits it into **global exertion** (RPE 6.5, breath cycle 1.25 s, recovery rate 0.025/s) and **local capacity** per region (e.g., left leg 0.46, right leg 0.78, right shoulder 0.63), then lists the coordination effects that must show up in later motion: increased step-width variability, longer stabilization after hard redirection, and greater trunk contribution when the right shoulder is taxed [S5].

## Injury: mechanical consequences plus compensations, with declared uncertainty

An injury object must specify mechanical effects (e.g., left knee: load acceptance 0.46, flexion tolerance 0.58, push-off capacity 0.52) and the compensations that follow (favoring right-leg support, shortening the left stance interval, increasing trunk lean during emergency recovery). The book insists the source is dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement, so confidence is declared (0.70) rather than assumed [S6]. A related stage-combat-voice discussion adds that pain alters breath and the voice's connection to pitch, rhythm, quality, resonance, and intensity, with injuries near the body's center tending to lower vocal pitch and peripheral injuries raising it — and that adrenaline can mask how serious an injury is [S11].

## How the book verifies these states are real controls

The verification apparatus is the telling part. Metrics include **uncaused state-change rate** (target 0 for hard facts — an advantage or injury must not flip without an event), **state persistence recall**, **beat causal completeness**, **affect-to-action coupling** (reported by character, explicitly avoiding stereotype scoring), **fatigue propagation**, and **injury compensation consistency** ("injured region performs at baseline without cause" is the failure state) [S2]. Invariants reinforce the same idea: an injury that begins at state.v2 persists through the final frame; no active contact disappears without an explicit release cause; no action boundary may discard support, root velocity, orientation, injury, ownership, or active contact [S12].

**In one line:** the book's position is that affect, fatigue, and injury earn the name "control states" only when they demonstrably change what the character does next — otherwise they are just labels.

What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
The sources treat **sound editing as the postproduction phase where the entire soundtrack is built and refined — and they rate it as harder than picture editing**, because more tracks mean more decisions and a direct line to whether the audience believes what it sees on screen [S1].

## Definition and role

Sound editing is where "all of these sound details are worked out": anything production didn't capture in original sound is created in postproduction [S1]. Once dialogue editing is finished, the creative process begins — the **sound designer**, whose input is compared to the director of photography's, takes responsibility for the overall acoustic experience and oversees the individual tracks, which include dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley [S8][S18]. The sound edit is more elaborate than the picture edit, and a wrong decision can readily undermine the visuals; in the book's words, "without an effective sound track, the visuals will not succeed" [S1]. Sound editing also appears as a distinct editing topic in the curriculum, listed alongside montage, compositing, color correction, and other editing topics [S13].

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
## The core advice

**Write sparely. Underwrite.** The book calls overwriting "the most common mistake people make in radio" and its blunt prescription is "Be a genius. Underwrite." [S3]. Sparse writing means fewer, tighter words that let the voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time — unless the concept genuinely demands a lot of words and fast action [S2][S16].

## Why it matters

- **Silence is radio's white space.** Bare-bones executions "leap out of the radio," and silence has remarkable power: it "enlarges the idea it surrounds," just as white space does in print [S10].
- **Time is already short.** Most spots are promotional, and clients often add their own promotional tags at the end, cutting further into your total time — so write sparely [S1]. A :30 is a different animal: if a 60-second spot is a house, a :30 is a tent, roughly 60 words [S21].
- **A fat script forces bad edits.** Showing up at the studio with a fat script means editing under pressure and without client approval [S4].

## Techniques from the book

1. **Time the mandatories first.** If the spot must close with legal copy — say, a bank commercial's "legal mumbo jumbo" — write it as sparely as possible and time it; the time left over is where your commercial has to fit [S3].
2. **Budget for the tags.** Reserve room at the end for clients' promotional tags [S1].
3. **Brainstorm concepts, not scripts.** Come up with many ideas and just scribble the general concept on a Post-it Note before writing any full script [S5].
4. **Let silence carry weight.** Structure the spot so quiet beats and pauses enlarge the idea rather than filling every second with words [S10].

## A model example

The book demonstrates the style itself: "Two unexpected ideas. Both create surprise. Radios are pieces of furniture, not something to slip into a pocket. Men don't walk on the moon. It's a long way up. The air is thin." [S9] — a few spare lines that leave the listener's imagination to fill in the wonder. That's the point: radio's canvas is large, so sparse writing can paint impossible scenes far too expensive to produce on TV [S15].
